P ∧ Q (and), P ∨ Q (or), ¬P (not), P → Q (implies), P ↔ Q (if and only if).

¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q and ¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ ¬Q. Negation flips the connective.
∀x P(x): 'for every x, P(x) holds.' ∃x P(x): 'there exists an x with P(x).' Order matters when mixed.
¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x). 'Not all users are admins' becomes 'there exists a user who is not an admin.'
A ⊆ B means every element of A is in B. {1,2} ⊆ {1,2,3} is true; {1,4} ⊆ {1,2,3} is false.

Assume the claim is false, derive a contradiction, conclude the claim is true. Classic: √2 is irrational.
If P then Q, where P is true, therefore Q. Firewall rules are modus ponens: 'if port-22-from-VPN then allow' + matched packet → allow.

cards.back: Deny rules are evaluated first (or a default-deny catches the rest): explicit deny beats allow, and anything unmatched by an allow is denied.

items.answer: Deny wins: explicit deny rules take precedence, and default-deny denies anything not explicitly allowed.

handsOnLab.brief: Build a tiny policy evaluator in Python that implements propositional logic over firewall rules: truth-table verification of De Morgan, a first-match-wins rule engine with allow/deny precedence, and a brute-force conflict check over a small packet space.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: De Morgan columns match on all rows; the engine's verdicts match your hand evaluations from the drills; the conflict checker correctly reports 'consistent' and, after you plant a conflicting rule, 'conflict found'.
handsOnLab.deliverable: policy-logic.py (truth-table checker, rule engine, conflict checker) + lab-notes.md (hand-vs-machine verdict comparison, one planted conflict and its diagnosis).
steps: Create ~/il29-m28-lab/policy-logic.py. Implement AND, OR, NOT, IMPLIES as Python functions on booleans.
Write a truth-table generator: for all 4 (P,Q) combos, print columns for ¬(P∧Q) and ¬P∨¬Q; assert the columns are identical.
Extend the generator to ¬(P∨Q) vs ¬P∧¬Q; assert identical. You have now machine-proved De Morgan.
Model a packet as a dict {port, src} and a rule as (condition_fn, action). Implement first-match-wins evaluation over an ordered rule list.
Encode the drill's three-rule policy (allow 22 from VPN; deny 23; allow 23 from admin-net) and evaluate: tcp/23 from admin-net → deny; tcp/22 from VPN → allow; tcp/80 from anywhere → default deny.
Add an explicit default-deny rule at the end and re-run; confirm unmatched packets are denied.

Write the brute-force conflict checker: enumerate a small packet space (ports {22,23,80} × src {vpn, admin, other} = 9 packets), evaluate each against the policy twice — once collecting 'allowed', once collecting 'denied' — and flag any packet in both sets.

Run the checker on the three-rule policy: expect 'consistent'. Then plant a conflicting rule (allow tcp/23 from any, placed before the deny) and confirm the checker reports the conflict with the exact packet.

Write lab-notes.md: your hand verdicts from drill 3 vs the engine's verdicts, and a paragraph diagnosing the planted conflict in logical terms (which rules, which packet, why first-match order created it).
Run the whole script fresh and confirm every assertion passes.
handsOnLab.title: Policy logic engine in Python

choices: Add the allow rule at the top so it matches first
Recognize first-match-wins semantics: the broad deny above shadows it — reorder or narrow the deny, then verify with a packet walk
Add a second identical allow rule below
mockTask.explain: First-match-wins makes rule order part of the policy's logic. A shadowed rule is dead configuration that confuses auditors; the fix is reordering or narrowing, verified by walking test packets through the engine.
mockTask.q: Panel question: a teammate's new allow rule 'isn't working' — packets it should permit are denied. You find a broad deny rule above it in a first-match-wins firewall. What do you tell them?

notes.body:
Security runs on logic, so you will learn logic properly — starting with propositions. A proposition is a declarative statement that is either true or false, never both, never neither. 'Port 22 is open on host A' is a proposition. 'Close port 22!' is not — it is a command. 'This statement is false' is not — it is paradoxical. Everything in policy evaluation, from firewall rules to allowlist decisions, is built from propositions joined by connectives. The five connectives: conjunction P ∧ Q ('and'), disjunction P ∨ Q ('or'), negation ¬P ('not'), implication P → Q ('if P then Q'), and biconditional P ↔ Q ('P if and only if Q'). Their meanings are fixed by truth tables — exhaustive enumerations of true/false combinations. Conjunction: true only when both sides are true. (T,T)→T; every other row →F. Disjunction: false only when both sides are false. (F,F)→F; every other row →T. Note this is inclusive or — 'coffee or tea' in logic means you may have both, unlike restaurant menus. Negation flips: ¬T=F, ¬F=T. Implication is the one that bites: P → Q is false in exactly one row — P true, Q false. A true premise cannot imply a false conclusion; every other combination is true, including the 'vacuous' rows where P is false. Worked example — the firewall reading: rule 'if the packet is from the VPN (P) then allow it (Q).' Packet from VPN that gets allowed: (T,T)→T, rule satisfied. Packet from VPN that gets denied: (T,F)→F, rule violated — this is the misconfiguration you hunt. Packet not from VPN that gets allowed by some other rule: (F,T)→T, this rule says nothing about it — a rule only constrains its own antecedent. Packet not from VPN, denied: (F,F)→T, rule vacuously satisfied. Internalize this: a rule 'if P then Q' never forbids ¬P cases; it only forbids the (T,F) row. Most firewall misreadings come from treating 'if P then allow' as 'only if P then allow' — the biconditional P ↔ Q, which is a much stronger claim (true exactly when P and Q match). Common mistake: reading implication as causation or as a promise about the false-antecedent rows. It is a truth function, nothing more — and that precision is exactly why it is useful.

Propositions live in your code, not just your policies. Every assertion is a proposition the programmer claims is true: assert user.is_authenticated states a proposition about program state. Preconditions and postconditions are implications: 'if the input is a valid packet (P) then the parser returns a struct (Q)' — and the (T,F) row is the bug you are hunting when the parser crashes on valid input. Type systems are propositional logic made mechanical: 'this variable is a non-null string' is a proposition the compiler tracks. The practical payoff: when debugging, translate the symptom into propositions and apply the truth tables. 'The rule should allow this packet but doesn't' becomes: rule-fires (P) is true, packet-allowed (Q) is false — the (T,F) row of the implication the rule promises, which means either the rule's antecedent doesn't actually match (P is secretly false — check the match fields) or something downstream overrides it. Logic doesn't just describe policies; it is the debugging discipline for every conditional in every system you will operate.
notes.title: Propositions and connectives: the atoms of policy

notes.body:
Two formulas are logically equivalent when their truth tables match on every row — same columns, same meaning, different syntax. Equivalence is what lets you rewrite policies confidently: if you can prove the rewrite preserves the truth column, the behavior is preserved. The most important equivalences are De Morgan's laws, and you will prove them here by hand because the proof technique — column comparison — is the general tool. Law 1: ¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q. Law 2: ¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ ¬Q. In words: negating a conjunction gives the disjunction of negations, and negating a disjunction gives the conjunction of negations — negation flips the connective. Proof of Law 1, all four rows. Row (T,T): P∧Q is T, so ¬(P∧Q) is F. Right side: ¬P is F, ¬Q is F, F∨F is F. Match. Row (T,F): P∧Q is F, negation T. Right: ¬P=F, ¬Q=T, F∨T=T. Match. Row (F,T): symmetric to previous — left T, right T. Match. Row (F,F): P∧Q is F, negation T. Right: ¬P=T, ¬Q=T, T∨T=T. Match. All four rows agree, so the equivalence holds — proved, no hand-waving. Law 2's proof is the mirror image; work it yourself row by row and confirm the columns match. Why operators care: De Morgan is how you negate compound conditions correctly. 'Not (admin AND from-VPN)' is not 'not admin and not from-VPN' — by Law 1 it is 'not admin OR not from-VPN.' Get this wrong in a policy and you invert who gets in: the buggy reading denies anyone failing either condition simultaneously... precisely, the buggy ¬P∧¬Q denies only people who are both non-admin and off-VPN, while the correct ¬P∨¬Q denies anyone who is non-admin or off-VPN — a much larger set. That is a real access-control bug shape, and it comes straight from mis-negating a conjunction. Also bank these equivalences: P → Q ≡ ¬P ∨ Q (implication as disjunction — check the columns), double negation ¬¬P ≡ P, and contrapositive P → Q ≡ ¬Q → ¬P. The contrapositive is your debugging friend: 'if the packet was allowed then it matched a rule' contraposes to 'if it matched no rule then it was denied' — the default-deny principle in logical dress. Common mistake: distributing negation without flipping the connective. Every time you negate across ∧ or ∨, the connective flips. No exceptions.

Make De Morgan a code-review checklist item, because the bug shape from this note appears constantly in real code. The pattern to grep for: any condition of the form !(a && b) or !(a || b), and any 'deny unless' policy translated into code. For each, verify the connective flipped. !(isAdmin && fromVPN) must become !isAdmin || !fromVPN — if you see && preserved, you have found the bypass. The same applies to query logic: 'NOT (status=active AND region=us)' in a filter means status!=active OR region!=us — the buggy AND version silently narrows the exclusion. Train yourself to expand negations aloud during review: 'not (A and B)' becomes 'not-A or not-B,' every time, until it is reflex. And when you write the condition yourself, prefer the positive form: instead of 'deny if not (admin and vpn),' write 'allow if admin and vpn; deny otherwise' — positive conditions with explicit default-deny are harder to mis-negate than clever negated compounds. Simplicity is a security control, and De Morgan is the tool that lets you see when a condition is more complex than it needs to be.
notes.title: Logical equivalence and De Morgan, proved by truth tables

notes.body:
Propositional logic handles fixed statements; predicates and quantifiers handle statements about collections — which is what policies are. A predicate is a parameterized proposition: Admin(x) is true or false depending on x. Quantifiers bind the parameter. ∀x P(x) — 'for all x, P(x)' — is true when P holds for every x in the domain. ∃x P(x) — 'there exists an x with P(x)' — is true when at least one x satisfies P. Worked examples in security language. ∀u (Access(u, db) → MFA(u)): 'every user with database access has MFA' — a compliance requirement as a formula. To falsify it you need one counterexample: a single user with access and no MFA. ∃p (Packet(p) ∧ Malicious(p) ∧ ¬Logged(p)): 'there exists a malicious packet that was not logged' — a detection-gap claim; to prove it you exhibit one. Negating quantified statements flips the quantifier — De Morgan generalized: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x), and ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x). Worked: negate 'all admins use hardware keys' (∀a (Admin(a) → HWKey(a))). Flip ∀ to ∃, negate the inside: ∃a ¬(Admin(a) → HWKey(a)). Since P→Q ≡ ¬P∨Q, ¬(P→Q) ≡ P∧¬Q: so ∃a (Admin(a) ∧ ¬HWKey(a)) — 'there exists an admin who does not use a hardware key.' That is exactly the audit finding you would write. Now the subtle part: quantifier order matters when they mix. ∀p ∃r (Packet(p) → Matches(p, r)): 'every packet matches some rule' — coverage, each packet may match a different rule. ∃r ∀p (Packet(p) → Matches(p, r)): 'some single rule matches every packet' — a universal rule, far stronger. Swapping them is a classic specification bug: a policy review that proves the first while the requirement demanded the second has proved the wrong thing. Worked domain example: 'every alert has an owner' (∀a ∃o Owns(o,a)) does not imply 'someone owns all alerts' (∃o ∀a Owns(o,a)) — the first is achievable with a rotation, the second demands a hero. Common mistake: reading ∃ as 'there exists a unique' — it means at least one. And treating ∀ over an empty domain: 'all zero of the firewall rules are correct' is vacuously true, which is why 'we have no rules and all our rules are correct' is the kind of true-but-alarming sentence auditors learn to distrust.

Quantifiers are also the tool for writing requirements that cannot be misread — which is a security skill, because ambiguous requirements become vulnerable implementations. Compare 'the system must authenticate users' with 'for every access request r, there exists an authentication check c that r passed before access was granted.' The second version pins down the quantifiers: every request, some check, and the ordering (check before grant). When a vendor says 'our product encrypts data,' ask the quantifier questions: for all data at rest? For all data in transit? Is there some data that is excluded? 'We encrypt customer data' might mean there exists some of it encrypted rather than all of it — and backups, logs, and caches are where the existential hides. Write your own security requirements with explicit quantifiers and explicit domains: 'for every production database d, for every network path p into d, p traverses the firewall' leaves no room for the 'oh, that replica wasn't in scope' surprise. The discipline feels pedantic until the first time it catches a scope gap that would have been a breach. Precision in requirements is prevention.
notes.title: Predicates, quantifiers, and their negations

notes.body:
Sets are the data structure of policy: allowlists, denylists, groups, and roles are all sets, and set operations are how you reason about them. A set is an unordered collection of distinct elements. x ∈ A means x is an element of A. A ⊆ B (A is a subset of B) means every element of A is in B. Worked small example: let Admins = {alice, bob}, VPNUsers = {bob, carol}, Contractors = {carol, dave}. Admins ∩ VPNUsers = {bob} — intersection, the users who are both. Admins ∪ Contractors = {alice, bob, carol, dave} — union. VPNUsers − Contractors = {bob} — set difference. Complement is relative to a universe: with universe U = {alice, bob, carol, dave}, the complement of Admins is {carol, dave}. These operations are the vocabulary of access reviews: 'who has access but shouldn't' is Granted − Authorized; 'who should have access but doesn't' is Authorized − Granted. A relation is a set of ordered pairs: R ⊆ A × B. {(alice, db1), (bob, db1), (bob, db2)} relates users to databases they may access. A function is a relation with a discipline: every input has exactly one output. {(alice, db1), (bob, db2)} is a function from users to primary databases; {(alice, db1), (alice, db2)} is not — alice maps to two outputs. Hash functions, encryption with a fixed key, and 'primary owner' assignments are functions; 'users who accessed' is a relation but not a function. Worked check: is 'manager of' a function from employees to employees? Only if every employee has exactly one manager — matrix management breaks it, which is why approval workflows built on 'the manager' need a tiebreak rule. Properties of relations you will meet: reflexive (every element relates to itself — 'same clearance level' is reflexive), symmetric (if a relates to b then b relates to a — 'is a peer of'), transitive (chains compose — 'can reach via network path' is transitive, which is exactly why lateral movement works: reachability composes). Equivalence relations (reflexive + symmetric + transitive) partition a set into classes — asset grouping by identical policy is an equivalence relation, and mis-grouped assets are equivalence-class errors. Common mistake: treating ordered pairs as unordered — (alice, bob) in 'reports to' is not (bob, alice). Direction is data.

Two applications deserve emphasis because you will use them weekly. First, equivalence classes for asset management: define 'same policy applies' as a relation — reflexive (an asset shares policy with itself), symmetric, transitive — and it partitions your fleet into classes. The operational win: you stop managing N assets and start managing k classes. The operational risk: a misclassified asset silently inherits the wrong policy, so audit class membership, not just the policies. Second, transitive closure for attack paths: 'can reach' is transitive, so the attacker's reachable set from a foothold is the transitive closure of the access relation — compute it and you have mapped lateral movement before the attacker does. Tools that do this (attack-path mapping) are just computing reachability over the relation your network defines. The defensive move is to break transitivity deliberately: segmentation, tiered credentials, and deny-by-default between zones exist to make 'can reach' non-transitive — A reaches B and B reaches C must not imply A reaches C. Every firewall rule between tiers is a statement that transitivity stops here.
notes.title: Sets, relations, and functions

notes.body:
Proofs are how you know something is true rather than merely plausible — and in security, 'plausible' gets people breached. Two techniques carry most of the weight. Direct proof: assume the premises, unfold definitions, compute, refold into the conclusion. Worked: prove the sum of two even integers is even. Let a and b be even. By definition, a = 2m and b = 2n for integers m, n. Then a + b = 2m + 2n = 2(m + n). Since m + n is an integer, a + b is twice an integer — even. Every step is definition or algebra; the proof is a straight line from premise to conclusion. Use direct proof whenever the definitions give you something to compute with. Proof by contradiction: assume the claim is false, derive something impossible, conclude the claim must be true. Worked — the classic: prove √2 is irrational. Assume otherwise: √2 = p/q for integers p, q with no common factors (lowest terms). Square: 2 = p²/q², so p² = 2q² — p² is even, so p is even (an odd square is odd), write p = 2k. Then (2k)² = 2q², so 4k² = 2q², q² = 2k² — q² is even, so q is even. But p and q both even contradicts lowest terms. The assumption is impossible; √2 is irrational. The shape — assume negation, push until contradiction — is reusable everywhere: 'assume this invariant can be violated, derive the violation's consequences, show they contradict a known fact.' Security-flavored example: prove that in a default-deny firewall, no packet is allowed without matching an allow rule. Assume a packet was allowed with no matching allow rule — but the engine only allows on rule match or default, and default is deny: contradiction. Therefore every allowed packet matched an allow rule. That two-line proof is an audit argument you can actually use: it tells you the complete evidence set for 'why was this allowed' is the matched rule. Common mistake: in contradiction proofs, forgetting what you assumed — write the assumption down and check every step against it. And in direct proofs, the classic error is using the conclusion as a step ('assume a+b is even... therefore...'). Proofs go from premises to conclusion, never the reverse.

Generalize the contradiction proof into the invariant method, your most powerful audit tool: to prove a system is safe, state the safety property as an invariant ('no packet crosses tiers without inspection'), assume a violation, and show the violation contradicts the mechanism. The firewall example from the note is the template — and it scales: 'prove backups cannot be encrypted by ransomware' becomes 'assume ransomware encrypted the backups; backups are immutable and offline, contradiction; therefore the assumption is impossible' — provided the immutability premise actually holds, which is what you audit. The method forces you to surface hidden premises: every contradiction proof rests on facts you assumed true, and in security those facts are the things attackers falsify (the 'immutable' backup that turned out to be writable, the 'offline' copy that was mounted). So the audit has two halves: the proof, and the verification of its premises. A proof with an unaudited premise is a hope with footnotes. Write both down — the invariant, the contradiction, and the evidence for each premise — and you have an audit argument that survives scrutiny instead of a checklist that survives no one.
notes.title: Proof techniques: direct and contradiction

notes.body:
Now apply the logic to the artifact you will actually operate: the policy. A firewall or allowlist policy is a set of if-then rules with a precedence discipline, evaluated against packets (or processes, or users). Two evaluation models dominate. First-match-wins: rules are ordered, the first matching rule decides, and evaluation stops. Here order is logic — swapping two rules can invert behavior. Worked example, three rules: R1: if tcp/22 from VPN then ALLOW. R2: if tcp/23 from any then DENY. R3: if tcp/23 from admin-net then ALLOW. Plus implicit default-deny. Packet: tcp/23 from admin-net. Walk: R1? Port is 23, no match. R2? Port 23 from any — match → DENY. R3 never evaluated. Verdict: DENY, even though a more specific allow exists below. The R3 rule is shadowed — dead configuration that misleads auditors into thinking admin-net has SSH-alternative access. The fix is reordering (R3 above R2) or narrowing R2 (deny 23 except admin-net) — and then re-walking test packets. Second model: precedence classes — all deny rules evaluated before allow rules (or vice versa), regardless of textual order. Here the logic is 'explicit deny beats allow; default-deny catches the rest,' which in formulas is: Allowed(p) ↔ (∃ allow-rule matching p) ∧ ¬(∃ deny-rule matching p). Worked: same packet under deny-first precedence — R2 (deny 23 any) matches → DENY, same verdict, but now no shadowing subtlety: precedence is explicit rather than positional. Translating policy questions into logic is the operator skill: 'is there a packet this policy both allows and denies?' becomes ∃p (Allowed(p) ∧ Denied(p)) — a satisfiability question over the rule set. If satisfiable, the policy is contradictory and the witness packet is your bug report. 'Does the policy allow anything it shouldn't?' becomes ∃p (Allowed(p) ∧ ¬Intended(p)) — which is why you write down Intended as a formula too. Common mistake: auditing rules without auditing order (first-match systems) or without stating the precedence model. A rule set is not a policy until the evaluation discipline is fixed — same rules, different discipline, different network.

Turn packet-walking into a test suite, because policies change and human re-walks do not scale. For every policy, maintain a set of test packets with expected verdicts: the obvious allows, the obvious denies, the boundary cases (the admin-net telnet from the drill), and at least one 'should be denied but looks innocent' case. Run the suite on every policy change — it is regression testing for firewalls. The suite also documents intent: a new team member reads the test packets and learns what the policy is for, which the raw rules never convey. Include negative tests for shadowing: a packet that should hit rule N but would be caught by rule M if reordered — if a future edit reorders rules, the test catches the shadow. And test the default: at least one packet matching nothing, asserting deny. The day someone 'temporarily' changes default-deny to default-allow for troubleshooting and forgets to revert it, that test is the alarm. Policies are code; treat them like code — versioned, reviewed, and tested. The logic in this module is the specification language; the test suite is the enforcement.
notes.title: Applying logic to policy evaluation

notes.body:
The final step: from hand-checking truth tables to letting a decision procedure do it — and understanding what that procedure is. SAT (satisfiability) asks: given a Boolean formula, is there an assignment of true/false to its variables that makes the whole formula true? If yes, the formula is satisfiable and the assignment is a witness; if no, it is unsatisfiable. This is not academic for you: 'does my firewall policy contain a conflict' is SAT. Encode each rule as a formula over packet variables (port = 23, src ∈ admin-net, ...), ask whether ∃p (Allowed(p) ∧ Denied(p)) is satisfiable, and a SAT solver hands you either 'no conflicts' or the exact packet that breaks the policy. You will build a brute-force version in the lab over a tiny packet space; industrial tools do the same thing with real solvers over enormous spaces. Two concepts make this practical. First, the formula shapes that stay easy: policies built from AND/OR/NOT over simple match conditions are exactly the fragment solvers devour — which is another reason to keep policies simple. Second, unsatisfiability as proof: when the solver says 'no conflict,' that is a proof of consistency, stronger than any amount of spot-checking. Worked miniature: rules 'allow tcp/22' and 'deny tcp/22' over packet variable port. Allowed(p) ↔ (port=22); Denied(p) ↔ (port=22). Conflict query: ∃p ((port=22) ∧ (port=22)) — satisfiable (p with port 22 is the witness): conflict confirmed. Add precedence 'deny beats allow': Allowed(p) ↔ (port=22) ∧ ¬(port=22) — unsatisfiable, so under deny-precedence the policy is consistent. The same two rules, consistent or not depending on the evaluation discipline — logic makes the dependence visible instead of tribal. Beyond SAT, know the landscape exists: SMT solvers handle richer theories (arithmetic, bit-vectors — your M29 bitmask questions are SMT-shaped), and model checkers verify stateful systems. You do not need to operate these tools today; you need to recognize when a problem is solver-shaped so you reach for the right tool instead of hand-auditing ten thousand rules. Common mistake: assuming 'the policy works because we tested some packets.' Testing samples; satisfiability proves. For the load-bearing policies, prove.

Know when a problem is solver-shaped and when it is not, because solvers are powerful within their envelope and useless outside it. Solver-shaped: static policy analysis ('is there a conflict?'), configuration verification ('does this ACL set permit the required flows and no others?'), bounded protocol checks. Not solver-shaped: anything with an adaptive adversary who changes the problem after seeing your solution (that is the arms race — the solver verifies a snapshot, the attacker moves), and anything where the model of the system is itself uncertain (a solver is only as good as its encoding; garbage in, proven garbage out). Also be honest about complexity: SAT is NP-complete, which sounds scary, but modern solvers handle millions of variables on structured problems like policies — the hardness is worst-case, and policy formulas are nicely structured. The practical limit is usually the encoding effort, not the solving time. Start with the lab's brute-force checker on small policies to build intuition, then graduate to real solvers when the policy outgrows enumeration. The mental shift that matters: from 'I tested some packets' to 'I asked whether a counterexample exists.' That question — asked routinely, answered by machine — is what separates audited policies from hoped-for ones.
